Purpose This study investigated the effect of performing hypoxic exercise at the same heart rate (HR) or work rate (WR) as normoxic exercise on post-exercise autonomic and cardiovascular responses. Methods Thirteen men performed three interval-type exercise sessions (5 × 5-min; 1-min recovery): normoxic exercise at 80% of the WR at the first ventilatory threshold (N), hypoxic exercise (FiO 2 = 14.2%) at the same WR as N (H-WR) and hypoxic exercise at the same HR as N (H-HR). Autonomic and cardiovascular assessments were conducted before and after exercise, both at rest and during active squat–stand manoeuvres (SS). Results Compared to N, H-WR elicited a higher HR response (≈ 83% vs ≈ 75%HRmax, p < 0.001) and H-HR a reduced exercise WR (− 21.1 ± 9.3%, p < 0.001). Cardiac parasympathetic indices were reduced 15 min after exercise and recovered within 60 min in N and H-HR, but not after H-WR ( p < 0.05). H-WR altered cardiac baroreflex sensitivity (cBRS) both at rest and during SS (specifically in the control of blood pressure fall during standing phases) in the first 60 min after the exercise bout ( p < 0.05). Post-exercise hypotension (PEH) did not occur in H-HR ( p > 0.05) but lasted longer in H-WR than in N ( p < 0.05). Conclusions Moderate HR-matched hypoxic exercise mimicked post-exercise autonomic responses of normoxic exercise without resulting in significant PEH. This may relate to the reduced WR and the limited associated mechanical/metabolic strain. Conversely, WR-matched hypoxic exercise impacted upon post-exercise autonomic and cardiovascular responses, delaying cardiac autonomic recovery, temporarily decreasing cBRS and evoking prolonged PEH. Keywords Hypoxic exercise Cardiac baroreflex sensitivity Heart rate variability Autonomic nervous system Post-exercise hypotension Hypoxia Università degli Studi di Verona Open access funding provided by Università degli Studi di Verona within the CRUI-CARE Agreement. issue-copyright-statement © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2021 Introduction In the past few years, hypoxic exercise (i.e. exercise combined with hypoxic stress) has been repeatedly highlighted as a promising nonpharmacological therapeutic intervention (Millet et al. 2016 ; Millet and Girard 2017 ; Lizamore and Hamlin 2017 ; Brocherie and Millet 2020 ). By reducing the mechanical load needed for adequate cardiovascular stimulation, hypoxic exercise represents a suitable option for obese and elderly patients to help meet exercise recommendations (Haufe et al. 2008 ; Girard et al. 2017 ; Pramsohler et al. 2017 ; Hobbins et al. 2017 ). Hypoxic exercise also has the potential to improve weight loss and cardio-metabolic health in overweight and obese patients (Netzer et al. 2008 ; Hobbins et al. 2017 ; Ramos-Campo et al. 2019 ), further representing a promising approach for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes prevention and treatment (Mackenzie et al. 2012 ; De Groote et al. 2018 ; Mai et al. 2019 ). Potential applications of hypoxic training in patients with various cardiovascular diseases, including hypertension, have also been highlighted (Wee and Climstein 2015 ). The present scenario suggests that the number of exercise training interventions including hypoxic exercise is likely to increase in the near future (Millet et al. 2016 ; Brocherie and Millet 2020 ). The interest in hypoxic exercise arises from its potential to promote greater physiological and health-related adaptions compared to normoxic exercise (Millet et al. 2016 ; Girard et al. 2020 ) in the long-term (i.e. chronic effects), stemming from the markedly different acute physiological responses (i.e. acute effects). At the same absolute work rate (WR), hypoxia-induced arterial chemoreceptor stimulation promotes greater sympathetic activation and withdrawal of parasympathetic activity (Hainsworth et al. 2007 ; Amann and Kayser 2009 ; Fisher 2015 ; Siebenmann et al. 2018 ), which lead to increased cardiovascular and ventilatory responses (Calbet et al. 2009 ; Sheel et al. 2010 ; Fisher 2015 ; Winkler et al. 2017 ) to cope with the lower blood oxygen content and to match metabolic demands (Bartsch and Gibbs 2007 ; Fisher 2015 ). Compensatory vasodilation of vascular beds facilitating blood and oxygen delivery to the working muscles also occurs (Joyner and Casey 2014 ; Dinenno 2016 ). As a result, the same absolute exercise intensity represents a greater physiological challenge in hypoxia (Mazzeo 2008 ; Fornasiero et al. 2019 ), which potentially affects post-exercise recovery responses (Luttrell and Halliwill 2015 ; Romero et al. 2017 ). An exacerbated increase of exercise-induced physiological stress of hypoxic exercise can result in delayed recovery of autonomic balance (i.e. progressive restoration of normal resting balance between parasympathetic and sympathetic activity) and altered post-exercise cardiovascular responses (Romero et al. 2017 ; Michael et al. 2017 ). Delayed parasympathetic recovery has been observed after hypoxic exercise conducted at similar absolute normoxic exercise intensity (Koelwyn et al. 2013 ; Fornasiero et al. 2018 , 2019 ). In addition, acute post-exercise blood pressure reduction (i.e. post-exercise hypotension, PEH) (Halliwill et al. 2013 ) may be intensified after hypoxic exercise (Horiuchi et al. 2016 , 2018 ; Saito et al. 2019 ) leading to an increased risk of orthostatic intolerance and hypotension (Halliwill et al. 2014 ) in the presence of an affected autonomic blood pressure control (i.e. impaired arterial baroreflex sensitivity). Previous studies investigated the impact of acute hypoxic stimuli on both cardiac and vascular sympathetic baroreflex sensitivity showing contrasting findings (Halliwill and Minson 2002 ; Roche et al. 2002 ; Gujic et al. 2007 ; Querido et al. 2011 ; Bourdillon et al. 2018 ; Simpson et al. 2019 ). However, while it seems that hypoxia may decrease cardiac baroreflex sensitivity (cBRS) (i.e. reduced reflex responsiveness) at rest and during exercise (Roche et al. 2002 ; Gujic et al. 2007 ; Bourdillon et al. 2017 , 2018 ), to the best of our knowledge, no study has investigated the impact of hypoxic exercise on post-exercise cBRS restoration. The timeframe for cBRS recovery depends on the physiological exercise intensity (Piepoli et al. 1993 ; Halliwill et al. 1996 ; Terziotti et al. 2001 ; Raczak et al. 2005 ; Reynolds et al. 2017 ), which is higher at the same absolute WR in hypoxia. Arguably, both the increased physiological exercise intensity relative to maximal, and hypoxic exercise per se, might negatively affect post-exercise cBRS responses, but this currently remains mere speculation. Indeed, no study has directly investigated post-exercise cBRS responses, comparing normoxic and hypoxic exercises performed at similar relative and absolute exercise intensities. Moreover, studies investigating the impact of hypoxia on cBRS during exercise only compared similar absolute exercise intensities (same WR) (Bourdillon et al. 2017 , 2018 ). In this regard, a better understanding of autonomic nervous system activity during recovery from hypoxic exercises of various intensities is of paramount importance especially because hypoxic exercise has been recommended amongst vulnerable populations (i.e., elderly and/or overweight/obese people, or suffering from diabetes or hypertension) who often exhibit altered autonomic cardiovascular control, and particularly cardiac baroreflex impairment (Lanfranchi and Somers 2002 ; Skrapari et al. 2006 ; Monahan 2007 ). Also, post-exercise recovery is a critical phase when sudden cardiovascular events are more frequent and often attributable to autonomic disturbances (Luttrell and Halliwill 2015 ). Interestingly, the hypoxia-induced increase in cardiovascular and ventilatory stimulation may be mitigated by matching to the exercise heart rate (HR) response (Winkler et al. 2017 ; Chacaroun et al. 2018 ; Fornasiero et al. 2019 ). By adjusting submaximal exercise intensity based on HR during exercise in hypoxia, ventilatory, anaerobic (i.e. blood lactate) and cardiac autonomic responses are similar to normoxic exercise (Zupet et al. 2009 ; Chacaroun et al. 2018 ; Fornasiero et al. 2019 ), and involve reduced mechanical load and aerobic demand (i.e. reduced VO 2 due to the decreased mechanical load). Similarly, blood pressure is reduced during hypoxic compared to normoxic exercise when HR is matched (Winkler et al. 2017 ). However, whether HR-matched hypoxic exercise leads to the same post-exercise responses is currently unknown. Thus, the aim of this study was to examine the effect of performing hypoxic exercise at the same relative (same HR) or same absolute (same WR) normoxic exercise intensity on the post-exercise cardiac autonomic and cardiovascular responses, while recovering in normoxic conditions. We hypothesised that moderate HR-matched hypoxic exercise would be associated with similar post-exercise autonomic and cardiovascular responses when compared to normoxic exercise, whilst WR-matched hypoxic exercise would result in delayed autonomic recovery and post-exercise cardiovascular responses dissimilar to normoxic exercise.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effect of heart rate-matched (HR-matched) or work rate-matched (WR-matched) hypoxic interval exercise on post-exercise cardiac autonomic and cardiovascular responses compared to normoxic exercise in moderately trained men. Findings indicate that HR-matched hypoxic exercise mimicked post-exercise autonomic responses of normoxic exercise without inducing significant post-exercise hypotension (PEH) or impairing cardiac baroreflex sensitivity (cBRS). Conversely, WR-matched hypoxic exercise resulted in delayed cardiac autonomic recovery, a temporary decrease in cBRS, and prolonged PEH.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed three interval-type exercise sessions (5x5-min work intervals; 1-min passive recovery) after a 5-min warm-up at 50% WR@VT1. Normoxic exercise (N) was at 80% of the work rate (WR) at the first ventilatory threshold (mean WR 183±19 W, mean HR 139±10 bpm, ~75%HRmax). Hypoxic exercise (FiO2 = 14.2%, simulating ~3000m altitude) was performed either at the same absolute WR as N (H-WR, WR-matched: mean WR 183±19 W, mean HR 154±11 bpm, ~83%HRmax) or at the same absolute HR as N (H-HR, HR-matched: mean WR 144±18 W, mean HR 138±9 bpm, ~75%HRmax). This resulted in a -21.1±9.3% reduction in WR for H-HR compared to N, and a higher HR (by ~15 bpm) for H-WR compared to N. Recovery was seated under normoxic conditions, with assessments at POST-15, POST-45, POST-60, and POST-90 minutes.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Cardiac Autonomic Indices (Heart Rate Variability, including RR interval, Ln-RMSSD, Ln-HF, Ln-SDNN, Ln-TP)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) derived metrics, physiological measurement

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cardiac parasympathetic indices were reduced 15 min after exercise and recovered within 60 min in N and H-HR, but not after H-WR (p < 0.05). Resting RR interval showed a greater decrease at POST-15 in H-WR compared to N (MD -91 ms, p=0.019) and H-HR (MD -110 ms, p=0.005). Ln-RMSSD decreased at POST-15 after N (MD -0.36 ms, p=0.041) and H-WR (MD -0.81 ms, p<0.001), remaining decreased at POST-60 only after H-WR (MD -0.29 ms, p=0.024). Ln-HF decreased after all sessions at POST-15 (p<0.05), remaining reduced after H-WR at POST-60 (MD -0.68 ms^2, p=0.036). Ln-SDNN decreased at POST-15 in N (MD -0.21 ms, p=0.045) and H-WR (MD -0.50 ms, p<0.001). Ln-TP decreased at POST-15 only in H-WR (MD -0.89 ms^2, p=0.006).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects cardiac beat-to-beat variability, vagal tone, and overall autonomic modulation, influencing heart rate and cardiovascular function, and promoting recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery after Normoxic (N), Heart Rate-matched Hypoxic (H-HR), and Work Rate-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions, assessed at various time points (POST-15, POST-60).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower values and delayed recovery indicate reduced vagal activity, increased sympathetic activity, or decreased autonomic flexibility, suggesting higher physiological stress and impaired cardiac autonomic recovery, particularly prolonged after H-WR.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: During work rate-matched hypoxic exercise (H-WR), HR was higher (~83%HRmax) compared to normoxic exercise (N, ~75%HRmax), an increase of approximately 15 bpm (p < 0.001). After exercise, a progressive decrease in HR is observed due to cardiac parasympathetic reactivation and sympathetic withdrawal.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiac activity and cardiovascular effort, mediating responses to meet metabolic needs during exercise and decreasing post-exercise due to autonomic recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During work rate-matched hypoxic exercise (H-WR) compared to normoxic exercise (N), and during post-exercise recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates physiological stimulation, cardiovascular stress during exercise, and the impact of exercise on autonomic recovery. Higher HR in H-WR suggests a greater physiological challenge.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced exercise WR (− 21.1 ± 9.3%, p < 0.001) compared to normoxic exercise (N) when heart rate was matched (H-HR).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents the mechanical load and energy expenditure during exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During heart rate-matched hypoxic exercise (H-HR) compared to normoxic exercise (N).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced mechanical load and limited associated mechanical/metabolic strain when heart rate is matched in hypoxia, impacting physiological stress.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Cardiac Baroreflex Sensitivity (cBRS), including Ln-cBRS TF, Ln-cBRS seq, Ln-cBRS seq+, and Ln-cBRS seq-
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Cardiovascular system (measured indirectly through heart rate and blood pressure responses)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Remained unchanged after HR-matched hypoxic exercise. Decreased at rest and during squat-stand manoeuvres (SS) in the first 60 min after WR-matched hypoxic exercise, recovering within 45 min. At rest, Ln-cBRS TF gain decreased at POST-15 only in H-WR (MD -0.28 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.004). Ln-cBRS seq decreased at POST-15 in H-WR (MD -0.32 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.027), and was significantly lower than H-HR (MD -0.37 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.045). Ln-cBRS seq+ and Ln-cBRS seq- at rest also decreased at POST-15 only in H-WR (MD -0.38 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.018 and MD -0.24 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.038, respectively). During SS, cBRS gain, phase, and coherence of transfer function analysis were unchanged across sessions (p>0.05), but Ln-cBRS seq- during SS decreased at POST-45 only with H-WR (MD -0.27 ms*mmHg^-1, p=0.030).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Autonomic control of blood pressure and heart rate, essential for maintaining cardiovascular homeostasis and responding to postural changes, buffering blood pressure changes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery after Normoxic (N), HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR), and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions, both at rest and during active squat–stand manoeuvres.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreased cBRS indicates impaired autonomic blood pressure control and reduced reflex responsiveness, increasing the risk of orthostatic intolerance and hypotension, particularly after WR-matched hypoxic exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PEH did not occur after heart rate-matched hypoxic exercise (H-HR) (p > 0.05). It was present after normoxic exercise (N) (-9 mmHg at rest 15 min post-exercise, and during SS manoeuvres 45 min post-exercise). PEH lasted longer in work rate-matched hypoxic exercise (H-WR) than in N (p < 0.05), still present 60 min post-exercise, and was greater during dynamic tasks following H-WR.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Acute reduction in blood pressure following exercise, influenced by central sympathetic outflow and local vasodilation, thereby influencing cardiovascular recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery after HR-matched, WR-matched hypoxic exercise, and normoxic exercise, both at rest and during dynamic tasks (squat-stand manoeuvres).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of cardiovascular recovery; absent PEH in H-HR may indicate lower physiological stress, while prolonged or greater PEH in H-WR suggests greater cardiovascular stress, delayed recovery, and increased risk of orthostatic intolerance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At rest, SAP decreased at POST-15 in N (MD -10 mmHg, p=0.005) and H-WR (MD -11 mmHg, p=0.001), and at POST-60 only in H-WR (MD -7 mmHg, p=0.043). During squat-stand (SS) manoeuvres, mean SAP decreased at POST-45 in N (MD -9 mmHg, p=0.010) and H-WR (MD -13 mmHg, p<0.001), with a greater decrease in H-WR compared to N (MD -9 mmHg, p=0.003). It remained decreased at POST-90 only in H-WR (MD -6 mmHg, p=0.018). Minimal SAP during SS decreased at POST-45 in N (MD -12 mmHg, p=0.002) and H-WR (MD -20 mmHg, p<0.001), with reduced values in H-WR compared to N (MD -15 mmHg, p<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the maximum pressure exerted on the arteries during heart contraction, indicating cardiovascular load and ensuring adequate perfusion.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest and during repeated squat-stand manoeuvres following Normoxic (N), HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR), and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A decrease indicates a post-exercise hypotensive response or impaired cardiovascular regulation during orthostatic challenges, particularly prolonged and more pronounced after H-WR, affecting postural stability.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At rest, DAP significantly increased at POST-60 in H-HR (MD 7 mmHg, p=0.002) compared to PRE. During squat-stand (SS) manoeuvres, DAP significantly decreased at POST-45 in H-WR (MD -4 mmHg, p=0.035) and increased at POST-90 in H-HR (MD 5 mmHg, p=0.017) compared to PRE.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the minimum pressure exerted on the arteries between heartbeats, reflecting vascular resistance and maintaining blood flow during diastole.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest and during repeated squat-stand manoeuvres following HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR) and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Changes suggest altered peripheral vascular resistance or cardiac output during recovery and orthostatic challenge, indicating varying cardiovascular regulation responses and potentially impacting cardiovascular recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At rest, MAP decreased at POST-15 in N (MD -5 mmHg, p=0.024) and H-WR (MD -4 mmHg, p=0.037). It increased at POST-60 in H-HR (MD 5 mmHg, p=0.017) compared to PRE, and was significantly lower in H-WR compared to N (MD -9 mmHg, p=0.044). During squat-stand (SS) manoeuvres, MAP decreased at POST-45 in N (MD -5 mmHg, p=0.031) and H-WR (MD -8 mmHg, p=0.001). It increased at POST-90 only in H-HR (MD 4 mmHg, p=0.042). At POST-45, MAP was significantly lower in H-WR compared to N (MD -7 mmHg, p=0.003) and H-HR (MD -5 mmHg, p<0.001), and compared to H-HR at POST-90 (MD -5 mmHg, p=0.018).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents the average arterial pressure during a single cardiac cycle, indicating overall tissue perfusion and cardiovascular load.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest and during repeated squat-stand manoeuvres following Normoxic (N), HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR), and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreases suggest post-exercise hypotension and impaired cardiovascular regulation during orthostatic challenges, while increases or differential responses indicate altered cardiovascular load and perfusion, depending on the exercise condition.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased at POST-60 compared to PRE (main effect for time p = 0.002) during seated recovery across all exercise conditions; no specific quantitative value provided beyond the p-value.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, crucial for delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest, specifically during seated recovery 60 min after exercise cessation across all conditions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A decrease indicates reduced efficiency of blood circulation or reduced demand during recovery, potentially impacting oxygen and nutrient delivery to tissues and overall cardiovascular efficiency.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly reduced at POST-15 and POST-60 compared to PRE (main effects for time all p < 0.001) during seated recovery across all exercise conditions; no specific quantitative value provided beyond the p-value.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Volume of blood pumped from the left ventricle per beat, a determinant of cardiac output, indicating cardiac pump efficiency.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest, specifically during seated recovery at POST-15 and POST-60 after exercise cessation across all conditions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A reduction indicates decreased cardiac contractility or venous return during recovery, potentially affecting circulatory efficiency, cardiac performance, and overall cardiovascular recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased at POST-15 in H-WR (MD -0.16 mmHg s mL^-1, p = 0.009) and increased at POST-60 in H-HR (MD 0.18 mmHg s mL^-1, p = 0.003) compared to PRE. Reduced TPR was also generally mentioned to indirectly support post-exercise autonomic alterations contributing to longer PEH after WR-matched hypoxic exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents the resistance to blood flow in the systemic circulation, impacting blood pressure and organ perfusion.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest after HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR) and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreases indicate vasodilation contributing to hypotension, while increases indicate vasoconstriction, both affecting blood pressure regulation and potentially tissue perfusion during recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased at POST-15 after all exercise sessions (time effect, p < 0.05) for both positive (n+) and negative (n-) sequences.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the frequency of baroreflex-mediated responses to blood pressure changes, indicating compensatory mechanisms.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery after Normoxic (N), HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR), and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions, at POST-15.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: An increase suggests a more frequent occurrence of baroreflex sequences during early recovery, indicating an active compensatory mechanism to regulate blood pressure.
